paper_title: AgentVQA: A Unified Benchmark for Agentic Visual Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are quickly becoming the decision-making core for agentic systems spanning
robotics, web navigation, or gameplay. By prompting or fine-tuning, VLMs often outperform their domain-
specific counterparts (Koh et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Sarch et al.,
2025) and serve as the backbone for top-performing action models (Black et al., 2026, 2025; Ji et al., 2025).
sections.content: In domains like mathematics and coding, standardized benchmarks have accelerated progress by systematically tracking model capabilities and reliably exposing performance gaps (Jimenez et al., 2023; Balunović et al., 2025). For agents, online evaluations in real or simulated environments remain the gold standard for assessing agentic performance (Yao et al., 2024), but due to computational cost and reproducibility, they present practical challenges for rapid, large-scale model comparison (Henderson et al., 2018; Dasari et al., 2022). As result, VLMs agentic capabilities lack comparable evaluation frameworks. State-of-the-art models are often assessed on general-purpose benchmarks like MMMU (Yue et al., 2025), MMBench (Liu et al., 2024) and GPQA (Rein et al., 2024). While these benchmarks assess broad vision-language and language understanding, their questions and visual inputs do not reflect agentic decision-making scenarios. They primarily assess general visual understanding or knowledge-intensive reasoning. Recent works (Yao et al., 2024; Yehudai et al., 2025; Wong et al., 2025) show that performance on general-purpose VQA benchmarks does not reliably correlate with success in agentic tasks. To address this, several domain-specific benchmarks have advanced evaluation of agentic capabilities within their respective settings (Koh et al., 2024; Rawles et al., 2024; Bonatti et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025b). However, these often provide narrow domain coverage, inputs and action spaces that do not reflect real agentic scenarios, or evaluation sets that are either saturated or affected by noisy annotations. We introduce AgentVQA, manually curated benchmark for systematically evaluating general-purpose VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios. AgentVQA contains 1,000 single-image, multi-frame, and video-based multiple-choice questions curated from 23 datasets across five domains: Web Agents, Egocentric Videos, Robotics, Games, and Spatial Planning. These domains represent distinct forms of agentenvironment interaction, including GUI navigation, temporally extended first-person understanding, embodied perception and action, strategic decision-making, and 3D spatial planning, as illustrated in Figure 1. By evaluating these settings within common benchmark, AgentVQA supports both aggregate model comparison and analysis of whether agentic capabilities generalize across domains. We construct AgentVQA through human-centered, model-assisted pipeline designed to provide broad coverage, standardized evaluation, and meaningful difficulty. VLMs screen candidates and propose hard distractors, while annotators select, repair, and verify every retained example. Only about 22% of the initial candidates survive the full curation pipeline, as human review identifies subtle ambiguities and annotation errors missed by automated checks and removes examples that are insufficiently challenging. The final benchmark expresses heterogeneous targets, including coordinates, actions, spatial relations, and predicted states, through common multiple choice interface while preserving the semantics of the original tasks. Model rankings on AgentVQA correlate with those from SpatialWorld (Gao et al., 2026), an online evaluation of agentic capabilities in simulation, supporting its use as scalable complement to interactive evaluation. At the same time, its rankings differ substantially from those on broad visual and reasoning benchmarks such as MMMU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, and ChartQAPro, suggesting that performance on conventional benchmarks does not reliably predict agentic competence. Across the 22 openand closed-source models we evaluate, the strongest model achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Moreover, the strongest model differs across domains, showing that aggregate performance can obscure substantial variation in domain-specific capabilities. Our cross-domain error analysis reveals shared limitation that manifests differently across agentic settings. Failures are dominated by grounded scene and state understanding: models struggle with UI localization in Web Agents, motion interpretation in Egocentric Videos, 3D spatial reasoning in Robotics and Spatial Planning, and visual state comprehension in Games. In contrast, failures arising from misunderstanding the task or selecting an answer inconsistent with the models reasoning are rare. These results suggest that current VLMs often understand the requested objective and can reliably reason over perceived inputs but fail to construct and maintain the grounded representation of the environment needed to act correctly. 2 Figure 2. sections.title:
2 Related Work
VLM as agents. Recent advances in multimodal AI have been driven by the development of Vision-Language
Models (VLMs). These models, such as QwenVL (Bai et al., 2023), GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), and
Gemini (Deepmind, 2026), are typically pretrained on vast, web-scale datasets of paired images and text.
This equips them with a broad general-purpose understanding of both visual concepts and natural language,
making them an ideal compute unit for agents. Several works have successfully adapted VLMs into specific
domains, either by fine-tuning or scaffolding pre-trained models (Black et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024; Zhou
et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Sarch et al., 2025). AgentVQA evaluates agentic capabilities across domains.
sections.content: General visual question answering. wealth of benchmarks have been developed to assess the general capabilities of VLMs, including SEED-Bench (Li et al., 2023a), MMBench (Liu et al., 2024), or MMMU (Yue et al., 2025). While invaluable for measuring core competencies and reasoning, they are ill-suited as proxies for agentic intelligence. Agentic tasks often require episodic memory (Majumdar et al., 2024) because either the modalities are iterative, e.g., stream of image observations, or the task requires interactive reasoning, e.g., tool-calling. Yao et al. (2024) found that GPT-4o, despite excelling on traditional benchmarks, achieves success rate less than 50% on realistic customer service tasks requiring multi-turn interactions. In Fig. 6, we confirm this observation by the divergence between rankings in AgentVQA vs MMMU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond. Agentic benchmarks. The agentic evaluation landscape spans language-only benchmarks, e.g., SWEbench (Jimenez et al., 2023) and AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023), which test capabilities such as code generation and tool use, and vision-language benchmarks requiring visual grounding and spatial reasoning. These benchmarks can also be categorized as online or offline. Online benchmarks, e.g., (Savva et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b; Koh et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), evaluate agents through environment interaction and therefore capture non-deterministic dynamics important for real-world deployment, but are often costly and infrastructure-intensive (Henderson et al., 2018; Du et al., 2024). Offline benchmarks, e.g., (Rawles et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025a; Team et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2025), instead use verifiable question-answer tasks paired with visual inputs. However, existing offline benchmarks are largely domain-specific and differ in answer formats, option difficulty, and sample distributions, making direct aggregation and cross-domain analysis difficult  (Table 4)  . AgentVQA is curated by filtering and transforming samples into standardized, unambiguous multiple choice format with hard negatives. 3 Figure 3. Dataset curation pipeline for AgentVQA. (1) Collect candidates across 23 datasets, task types, and input modalities spanning five agentic domains. (2) Standardize tasks as MCQs; Gemini 2.5 Pro proposes three hard negatives when needed. (3) Gemini and Claude flag ambiguity, annotation errors, and weak distractors, removing approximately 45% of candidates. (4) Human annotators review, edit, and repair the remaining samples, rejecting approximately 60% as ambiguous, incorrect, or too easy. (5) Verify exactly one correct answer and plausible, unambiguously incorrect hard negatives, then assemble 1,000 manually verified questions balanced across the five domains.

sections.title:
3 The AgentVQA Benchmark
We define agentic tasks as those that evaluate action selection or the perceptual and reasoning capabilities
required for goal-directed interaction with an environment Bengio et al. (2025). To support scalable offline
evaluation of these capabilities, AgentVQA comprises 1,000 manually curated multiple-choice questions drawn
from 23 datasets spanning five agentic domains. Its construction is guided by three principles: comprehensive
coverage across domains to assess skill generality; standardized evaluation using manually curated questions
with unambiguous ground truth; and challenging examples, states, and negative options designed to expose
fine-grained weaknesses in current models.
sections.content: To provide comprehensive coverage, AgentVQA spans five distinct forms of agent-environment interaction: digital interaction and GUI navigation in Web Agents; embodied perception and action in Robotics; temporally extended first-person planning in Egocentric Videos; strategic decision-making in Games; and spatial navigation and planning in Spatial Planning. The benchmark is balanced across domains, with 200 questions per domain (Figure 2). Its inputs range from individual screenshots and embodied-scene images to multi-frame trajectories, egocentric videos, and gameplay videos. Heterogeneous targets, including coordinates, actions, spatial relations, and predicted states, are represented through common multiple-choice format while preserving observations of the agentic scenario. See Appendix for full details of the datasets.

sections.title:
3.1 Data Curation and Construction
We construct AgentVQA through a five-stage, human-centered pipeline. VLMs assist with large-scale screening
and hard-negative generation, while human annotators determine which examples are retained and verify the
correctness, clarity, and difficulty of every final question.
sections.content: Stage 1: Candidate collection. We assemble diverse candidate pool from 23 source datasets spanning five agentic domains (see Appendix for full dataset list). Candidates are sampled across datasets, task types, and input modalities to cover broad range of realistic observations, states, and decisions, while initially retaining their original questions, annotations, and answer formats. Stage 2: MCQ construction. We convert the candidate tasks into common multiple-choice format. For examples that are not originally multiple choice, Gemini 2.5 Pro proposes three hard negative options using the visual input, task prompt, correct answer, action history, and relevant task metadata. The generated distractors include both near-miss negatives, which differ from the correct answer in fine-grained way, and semantically similar negatives, which correspond to plausible but incorrect objects, actions, or locations. Stage 3: VLM-assisted screening. We use multi-turn verification pipeline with Gemini and Claude to identify converted questions with ambiguous instructions, inconsistent annotations, multiple plausible answers, malformed states, implausible distractors, or other quality issues. This high-recall screening removes approximately 45% of the initial candidate pool, reducing the amount of manual review required while preserving human judgment for cases involving subtle visual or domain-specific ambiguities. 4 Figure 4. Ambiguities addressed by manual curation (Stage 4, Section 3.1). (a) rectangular bounding box around scissors includes background, allowing clicks that miss the object to be scored as correct. (b) For the goal of deleting Lyft account, (green) directly opens Lyft and is the intended next action. However, can also lead to valid solution by opening the app drawer and then launching Lyft, adding navigation step. The question does not require the shortest route, leaving multiple plausible next actions. Manual review removes or repairs such ambiguous samples to ensure unique correct answer. Stage 4: Manual curation and repair. Human annotators then inspect the remaining candidates for correctness, difficulty, diversity, and relevance to agentic decision-making. Approximately 60% of the samples that pass automated screening are still rejected because they contain subtle ambiguities, annotation errors, invalid distractors, or are insufficiently challenging. When possible, annotators repair promising examples by refining the question, ground-truth answer, visual input, answer choices, or associated metadata before retaining them for the final evaluation format. Stage 5: Human verification and benchmark assembly. Every completed MCQ is manually reviewed second time to ensure that exactly one answer is correct and that the distractors are plausible, challenging, and unambiguously incorrect. This step along with Manual Curation is especially important for grounding tasks, where bounding boxes and automatic spatial checks can admit false positives or reject valid interaction points, as illustrated in Figure 4. We revise questions, annotations, and options as needed, then assemble balanced final benchmark of 1,000 manually verified questions, with 200 examples per domain and 40 or 50 examples from each source dataset.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models. We evaluate diverse suite of 22 prominent VLMs to ensure comprehensive assessment of the current landscape. Our selection includes closed-source models: GPT-5.6-sol thinking-high/none (OpenAI, 2026), GPT-5.6-luna thinking-high/none (OpenAI, 2026), GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026) and 3.7 Flash (Deepmind, 2026), Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026a) and Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), and Qwen3.7 Plus and Flash (Qwen Team, 2026b). We also include wide range of open-source models: the GLM series (4.6V (Z.AI, 2025), 4.5V (GLM-V Team, 2026), 4.1V-9B-Thinking/Base (GLM-V Team, 2026)), Kimi K3 (Team, 2026), Llama 4 Maverick (Meta, 2025), the Qwen3.5 series (397B-A17B, 122B-A10B, 35B-A3B, 27B) (Qwen Team, 2026a), and Qwen3.8 27B (Qwen Team, 2026c). 5 Models are categorized as Reasoning or Non-Reasoning based on whether they allocate extended token budgets for internal chain-of-thought reasoning before producing final answer. Evaluation setup. For models that do not natively support video input, we sample 32 frames at evenly spaced intervals. This number is validated by our own ablation studies and prior work (Yang et al., 2025a). Models are evaluated with temperature of 0.8 and 0.2 for reasoning and non-reasoning models, respectively. For models without manual temperature like GPT series, we use the default. We use standard prompt that provides the question and any relevant context, querying the model to output only the single letter corresponding to its choice. For questions involving spatial coordinates, options are formatted in each models native convention (e.g., normalized [0, 1000] in (y, x) order for Gemini, absolute pixel coordinates for Qwen). Final answers are extracted programmatically, and all visual inputs are provided at native resolution. Further details on prompts and answer extraction are in Appendices and E. sections.title: 4.2 Results on AgentVQA
sections.content: We report the results on AgentVQA in Table 1. We draw the following conclusions: Top models struggle with AgentVQA. Even the top performing model, Gemini 3.7 Flash, achieves only 58.5% accuracy. clear tiering is observable: the largest proprietary models (GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro) are at the top, followed by other competitive models such as Qwen3.7 Flash and the open-weight Qwen3.8 27B, with smaller and older-generation models in the lower tiers. Among the five domains, models perform best on Egocentric Videos and Games, followed by Spatial Planning, Robotics, and worst on Web Agents. This indicates that current VLMs are stronger at temporally contextualized visual understanding and game-state reasoning than at precise GUI grounding and spatial reasoning. Large variance per domain. Current VLMs are strongest on temporally grounded understanding (Egocentric Videos: 59%, Games: 51.5%) and weaker on precise grounding and embodied reasoning (Spatial Planning: 6 46%, Robotics: 38%, Web Agents: 29%). Web Agents is the hardest domain, with only three models exceeding 40%. Games exhibits the largest spread (23% to 70%), suggesting strategic reasoning is strong only in the most capable models. No single model dominates across all domains: Gemini 3.7 Flash leads Games (70%) but falls behind GPT-5.6-sol thinking-high in Web Agents (40.5% vs. 47%), while Qwen3.7 Flash leads Egocentric Videos (72.5%) and Gemini 3.7 Flash leads Spatial Planning (62.5%) and Robotics (52.5%). These cross-domain rank shifts indicate highly uneven capabilities across different settings. Open-source models are catching up. The gap between closed-source and open-source models remains narrow. The top closed-source model, Gemini 3.7 Flash (58.5%), leads the top open-source model, Qwen3.8 27B (50.9%), by 7.6%. Kimi K3 (48.3%), Qwen3.5 35B (47.9%), and Qwen3.5 397B (47.8%) outperform Claude Opus 4.8 (44.0%) and Sonnet 5 (43.4%). Multiple open-source models also substantially outperform GPT5.6-sol thinking-none (38.2%) and GPT-4o (31.4%). These results suggest that while the strongest proprietary models retain an advantage on agentic tasks, competitive open-source alternatives already match many closed-source systems. Reasoning offers varying results. Extended reasoning helps some models but not others. GPT-5.6-sol gains 16.8 points with thinking-high, while GLM 4.1V performs worse with thinking as compared to without it. We find that GLM-4.1V-Thinking gets stuck in thinking loops (App. J). Figure 5. Impact of action history on model performance in Web Agents. Trajectory questions benefit from action history. Our ablation on Web Agents tasks reveals that providing action history is consistent benefit (Figure 5). Across five models (Gemini 3.1-pro, GPT-4o, Qwen3.5 27B, Kimi K3, and Claude Sonnet 5), removing the history decreases average performance by 9.5% on AitW and 10% on MONDAY. This confirms that access to historical context is critical for multi-step tasks. Figure 6. Divergence in model performance rankings between AgentVQA and three existing benchmarks. Lines are colored red if models rank degrades and purple if it improves. The rank divergence shows that our benchmark has moderate-to-weak correlation with general VQA benchmarks. While few models maintain their ranks, the relative positions of most others change. In the comparison with GPQA-Diamond, no model maintains its relative ranking.

sections.title: 4.3 Rank Correlation
sections.content: Low correlation with existing benchmarks. To validate the benefit of specialized agentic benchmark, we compare model rankings for subset of models on AgentVQA to those on subset of MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2025) (250 samples), ChartQA-Pro (Masry et al., 2025) (250 samples), and GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024) (150 samples), running our own evaluations with standardized prompts. As shown in Figure 6, rankings diverge substantially. Spearmans rank correlation coefficients are moderate for MMMU-Pro (𝜌 = 0.67) and GPQA-Diamond (𝜌 = 0.59), and weak for ChartQA-Pro (𝜌 = 0.44). 7 No single model dominates across all comparisons. Gemini 3.1 Pro ranks second on AgentVQA and MMMUPro but drops to 5th on GPQA-Diamond, while Qwen3.8 27B leads GPQA-Diamond but falls to 6th on MMMU-Pro. These shifts confirm that strong performance on general-purpose visual reasoning does not reliably predict agentic competence. Figure 7. AgentVQA ranks models the way an online interactive benchmark does. (b) Model rankings under AgentVQA Spatial Planning against the SpatialWorld Physical track (𝜌 = 0.895, 𝑝 = 8 105). sections.title: 4.4 Correlation with Online Agent Evaluations
sections.content: To examine whether AgentVQA provides reliable alternative to costly interactive evaluation, we compare its model rankings with performance on SpatialWorld (Gao et al., 2026), closed-loop benchmark for embodied and interactive agents. SpatialWorld scores are obtained from the official released evaluation results, which are produced under single simulator-agnostic protocol across eight simulation backends. For this comparison, we separately evaluate 12 models from SpatialWorld on AgentVQA and compare their relative rankings via Spearmans rank correlation. This analysis measures whether AgentVQA preserves the model ordering observed under interactive evaluation despite operating entirely offline and avoiding environment configuration and execution-related computational costs. Figure 7 shows strong positive Spearman rank correlation of 𝜌 = 0.895 across 12 overlapping models between SpatialWorld and AgentVQA Spatial Planning, the closest category. This agreement demonstrates that AgentVQA provides reliable and substantially lower-cost offline alternative for ranking agentic models, avoiding the environment setup, repeated rollouts, and computational expense required by online evaluation. The lower correlations for other AgentVQA domains suggest that model rankings depend on the capabilities being assessed, highlighting the limitations of single dataset as proxy for overall agentic performance. Together with the strong agreement in the matched domain, this pattern supports the interpretation that AgentVQA captures meaningful domain-specific performance differences.

sections.title: 4.5 Error Modes
sections.content: To understand why models fail, we analyze incorrect predictions from Gemini 3.1 Pro, sampled evenly across datasets. We prompt the model to provide its reasoning with each answer, manually establish taxonomy of common failure modes, and use Gemini to categorize the errors. We then manually review randomly selected subset with 100 error mode assignments in total across the five domains. For Gemini 3.1 Pro, the results reveal domain-specific manifestations of shared weakness: constructing an 8 Figure 8. Distribution of the most common error modes across the five agentic domains in AgentVQA. The analysis is based on semi-automated categorization of the incorrect predictions from Gemini-3.1-Pro. The chart is organized by domain, with each colored segment representing primary domain. Each bar within segment corresponds to specific error mode, and its size reflects its prevalence (%). accurate task-relevant state from visual observations (Figure 8). Among the analyzed incorrect Web Agents predictions, 78% were classified as grounding errors, indicating difficulty locating the correct interface element. All percentages refer to the distribution of error categories among analyzed incorrect predictions within each domain. In Games, visual miscomprehension (71%) shows that failures primarily arise from reading the game state rather than applying its rules. Robotics and Spatial Planning are dominated by spatial confusion (65%) and viewpoint gaps (62%), respectively, exposing weaknesses in relational and perspective-aware reasoning. Errors in Egocentric Videos are more distributed across motion misperception (39%), perception gaps (29%), and spatial confusion (15%), reflecting difficulty tracking dynamic states. Across domains, failures therefore arise mainly before high-level planning, during perception, grounding, and state construction. Additional details are provided in Appendix G.

sections.title:
5 Conclusion
We introduce AgentVQA, a unified offline benchmark that consolidates 23 datasets across five agentic domains
into 1,000 manually verified multiple-choice questions with challenging hard negatives. While prior work
typically evaluates agents within individual environments or domains (Koh et al., 2024; Rawles et al., 2024;
Bonatti et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b), AgentVQA enables controlled comparison of visual decision-making
capabilities across diverse agentic settings.
sections.content: Our results show that these capabilities remain far from solved: among 22 state-of-the-art VLMs, the strongest model achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our analysis of Gemini 3.1 Pros incorrect predictions identifies grounding, perception, motion understanding, and spatial state construction as the predominant error categories. Action history improves performance, while reasoning benefits some models but not others. However, neither closes the remaining gap. Moreover, AgentVQA rankings diverge from traditional VQA benchmarks while correlating strongly with SpatialWorld, suggesting that conventional benchmarks do not fully capture agentic readiness and that AgentVQA offers reliable, substantially lower-cost alternative for rapid agent-model evaluation. Taken together, these findings support viewing agentic competence as collection of domain-specific capabilities rather than single general ability. The strong agreement with online evaluation in the matched domain, alongside weaker cross-domain agreement, suggests that AgentVQA can help distinguish these capabilities and guide more targeted model development. Within the broader evaluation landscape, controlled offline benchmarks can complement interactive environments by identifying weaknesses efficiently and directing subsequent online testing toward the domains and failure modes that require closer investigation. Future work should connect specific offline error patterns to failures during interactive execution. Such analyses could guide improvements in grounding and state tracking while testing whether gains on controlled questions translate into more reliable online behavior.

Dataset Selection and Curation Rationale The construction of AgentVQA is guided by principled selection process to ensure the final benchmark is comprehensive, robust, and effective for evaluating the agentic capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Our domains: Web Agents, Egocentric Videos, Robotics, Games, and Spatial Planning are chosen to represent broad spectrum of agentic challenges, from digital interaction to embodied physical perception and strategic planning. The following five criteria are central to our selection of the 23 source datasets. High agentic signal. primary requirement is that each datasets tasks must involve strong agentic signal. This means moving beyond passive visual question answering (e.g., What color is the car?) to scenarios that demand active reasoning from an agents perspective. We prioritize datasets where the core task involves: Choosing actions or predicting the next optimal step. Evaluating the consequences of sequence of actions. Understanding causality and the relationships between actions and outcomes. Strategic planning toward specific goal. This focus ensures that AgentVQA directly probes the decision-making and reasoning capabilities that are fundamental to agentic intelligence. Comprehensive and distinct domain coverage. To test for generalist agentic behavior, we select datasets that span diverse domains and modalities. Each of the five chosen domains introduces unique set of challenges and required skills not fully covered by the others: Web Agents: Tests GUI navigation, grounding, and interaction in digital environment. Robotics & Egocentric Videos: Evaluate embodied perception, spatial awareness, and understanding of the physical world from first-person perspective. Games: Focus on strategic decision-making, reward modeling, and long-term planning in rule-based environments. Spatial Planning: Assesses foundational spatial awareness and reasoning, critical component for any embodied agent. 14 This multi-domain approach prevents the benchmark from being too narrow and allows for holistic assessment of VLMs generalization ability. Offline convertibility. crucial practical consideration is the feasibility of converting each dataset into standardized, offline format. This criterion requires that the source data (e.g., trajectories, videos) be sufficiently structured to allow for an unambiguous conversion into Multiple-Choice Question (MCQ) format. Every resulting MCQ must have single, verifiably correct answer to enable scalable, deterministic, and efficient evaluation without relying on resource-intensive online simulators. Public availability and permissive licensing. To ensure transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility for the broader research community, all selected datasets must be publicly available. Furthermore, their licenses must permit modification and redistribution as part of new benchmark, allowing us to legally and ethically create and share AgentVQA. Sufficient scale. The selected datasets need to be large enough to provide diverse pool from which highquality samples can be curated. larger source pool increases the likelihood of finding samples that are both challenging and unambiguous across range of question types. This criterion ensures that our manual curation process (Section 3.1) has adequate coverage of each domain and dataset. Every output is represented as multiple choice question, while the listed output type identifies the meaning of the selected option. Hard Negative Generation Pipeline The difficulty of AgentVQA is ensured by systematic process for generating challenging distractor options, or hard negatives. This process transforms tasks that are not inherently multiple-choice, such as web navigation trajectories, into standardized and rigorous MCQ format. Our pipeline creates negatives that are both plausible and unambiguously incorrect, forcing models to demonstrate fine-grained understanding rather than relying on simple heuristics. The process is detailed below. VLM-assisted generation. To select the generation model, we first conducted preliminary study on data subset using Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o, and Qwen 2.5 VL (7B). After manually comparing the generated samples for both difficulty and accuracy, we selected Gemini 2.5 Pro for its superior performance. We therefore employ VLM-assisted pipeline centered around Gemini 2.5 Pro to generate hard negatives. For each question, we provide the model with comprehensive context, including the primary image or screenshot, the task prompt, the ground-truth answer, any relevant action history for sequential tasks, and metadata such as image dimensions and coordinate formats (e.g., (x,y) for points, or (𝑥1, 𝑦1, 𝑥2, 𝑦2) for bounding boxes). For grounding tasks, we also visually render the correct actions location onto the image. Given this context, we prompt the model to generate three distinct hard negatives as combination of two types: near-miss negatives and semantically similar negatives. Near-miss negatives are distractors spatially close to the correct answer that test precision, such as coordinates few pixels away from correct UI element. Semantically similar negatives are conceptually related to the correct answer and test the models ability to differentiate between similar objects, such as choosing Mobile phone when the correct answer is Tablet. The exact prompt used for generating these hard negatives is in Appendix Verification and filtering. To ensure quality, the generated negatives undergo two-stage verification process. First, an automated script filters grounding-based distractors by verifying their coordinates fall outside the ground-truth bounding box, programmatically confirming the option is negative. Following this, subset of these samples undergoes rigorous manual review. We manually verify each distractor for both plausibility, ensuring the option is believable choice that could confuse model, and unambiguous incorrectness, which guarantees there is only one correct answer to the MCQ. This human-in-the-loop step is critical for ensuring the quality of the generated negatives prior to the manual curation stage described in Section 3.1. Definition of Agentic Tasks The community defines agentic tasks as those requiring system to "observe their environment and act in it in order to achieve goals" Bengio et al. (2025), encompassing perception to sense the state, intelligence to reason and plan, and affordances to execute actions Plaat et al. (2025). While traditional image VQA treats visual understanding as an end in itself, agentic VQA frames perception as means to action. Here, each answer must inform executable decisions rather than merely describe what is seen Reed et al. (2022). To ensure AgentVQA captures this full capability range, we structure our sub-tasks into unified hierarchy: Action Grounding tasks (e.g., Tap) test the critical translation of semantic intent into executable spatial actions Reed et al. (2022); Spatiotemporal Reasoning tasks evaluate the dynamic mental maps required for movement; State Understanding tasks (e.g., Functional Reasoning) ensure the agent can accurately parse the environment to inform decision-making; and Strategic Planning tasks (e.g., Reward Modeling) assessing long-term outcomes through multi-step reasoning Sutton et al. (1998). Answer Extraction Logic To ensure consistent and automated evaluation, we employ multi-strategy answer extraction logic. Although the prompt instructs models to output only single letter corresponding to their final choice, outputs can vary. Our programmatic parser is designed to robustly handle these variations. Extraction strategy. The extraction process follows prioritized sequence of rules. First, our parser attempts direct match, checking if the models entire stripped output is exactly single, valid option letter (e.g., A). If this primary strategy fails, it deploys fallback routine that applies series of regular expression patterns. These patterns are designed to find common answer declarations such as Answer: A, or Option A. We note that these regular expressions are occasionally adapted to accommodate the unique, consistent output formats of specific models. If no unambiguous answer can be identified after applying all strategies, the question is skipped and marked unevaluated to maintain the integrity of the evaluation. The complete prompt is available in Appendix K. Robustness Analysis of MCQ Format To ensure the reliability of the multiple-choice format, we conducted extensive ablation studies to quantify the impact of option ordering and rule out random guessing as confounding factor. Robustness to Option Ordering. We evaluated 5 representative models across 6 datasets using 5 distinct, seeded random permutations of option orders. As shown in Table 3, the model performance remains highly consistent across permutations, with standard deviation of approximately 1.9%. This confirms that the rankings reported in AgentVQA are stable artifacts of model capability rather than positional bias. To verify that model scores reflect genuine engagement with the task, we evaluated constant-selection baselines (e.g., Select All A, Select All B) across the benchmark. These strategies yielded accuracies of 28% (A), 27% (B), 23% (C), and 22% (D), averaging 25.0%, which aligns with the theoretical random baseline for 4-option MCQs. Since all 22 models in Table 1 achieve overall accuracies above the 25% random-guessing baseline (lowest: 28%), we conclude that AgentVQA measures performance beyond chance at the full-benchmark level. 17 Error Modes To qualitatively understand model failures, we conduct an in-depth error mode analysis on Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026). The process involves three-stage methodology to develop taxonomy, annotate failures, and verify the results. The resulting distribution of errors is visualized in Figure 8. Taxonomy development and annotation. First, we prompt the model to output reasoning chain alongside its final answer for every question. We then manually review diverse, stratified subset of incorrect predictions to identify and define comprehensive taxonomy of common failure patterns for each of the five agentic domains. With this taxonomy established, we use Gemini 3.1 Pro for large-scale annotation. For each failure, we provide the model with the visual input, all multiple-choice options, the ground-truth answer, the models incorrect chosen option, the models full reasoning chain, and any other relevant metadata. We then prompt it to assign the single most fitting error mode from our predefined taxonomy. The prompt used for assigning error modes is available in Appendix M. Verification. To ensure the quality of the automated annotations, we perform final verification step. We manually review randomly selected subset with 100 error mode assignments across all domains. This process confirms that the classifications are accurate and consistent with our established definitions, ensuring the reliability of our qualitative analysis. G.1 Error Mode Definitions Web Agents. Grounding Error occurs when the model understands the goal but fails to correctly locate or ground the corresponding UI element, often confusing it with visually similar or nearby one. Logical Breakdown describes failure to correctly process sequence of steps, leading to logically inconsistent action based on the current state. Visual Hallucination is when the models reasoning relies on UI element or piece of information that is not present in the visual input. Missing Inference occurs when the model fails to deduce an implicit but necessary action, such as scrolling to reveal an element. Action Mismatch happens when the models reasoning correctly identifies the right action, but its final output selects different, incorrect option. Goal Misunderstanding is fundamental error where the model misinterprets or ignores key part of the users instruction. Egocentric Videos. Motion Misperception occurs when the model fails to correctly interpret process, motion, or physical interaction as it unfolds over time. Perception Gaps are fundamental failures in seeing, where the model incorrectly reports basic, static fact like an objects presence or count. Spatial Confusion is failure to build an accurate 3D mental map from video, resulting in an incorrect understanding of object layout or orientation from given viewpoint. Incomplete Analysis happens when the model perceives all necessary visual facts but fails to execute the required logical steps to reach the correct conclusion. Task Misinterpretation arises when visual perception is correct, but the model misunderstands the nuance or goal of the prompt. Robotics. Spatial Confusion occurs when the model fails to correctly interpret the spatial relationships, location, or orientation of objects in 3D space from 2D image. Object Misrecognition happens when the model misidentifies an object or fails to ground it based on all of its required attributes like color or size. Action-Time Disconnect is failure to understand the dynamics of scene, such as predicting the outcome of an action or correctly sequencing task. Selection Error occurs when the models reasoning arrives at the correct conclusion, but it selects the wrong option in its final output. COT Failure describes cases where the chain-of-thought reasoning process breaks down, failing to handle specific quantitative values or fine-grained distinctions. Games. Visual Miscomprehension is foundational failure to correctly perceive the games visual and spatial information, such as object locations or relationships. Rule Misunderstanding is logical error where the model does not correctly apply the games explicit rules or objectives. Tracking Drift is failure to mentally simulate and track how the game state changes over time. Reasoning Breakdown is general failure where the models internal logic collapses under the tasks complexity or becomes confused about the objective, leading to flawed conclusion. Context Hallucination occurs when the models reasoning becomes detached from the game state, inventing information that does not exist. 18 Spatial Planning. Viewpoint Gap occurs when the model identifies objects but fails to construct an accurate 3D map of their relationships, leading to errors in judging depth or distance. Categorization Confusion occurs when perception is visually correct, but the model applies the wrong semantic label or category to an object. Detection Hallucination is fundamental perceptual failure where the model either misses present object or sees an object that is not there. Logic Collapse is failure cascade where the model first fails to perceive an object and then tries to compensate by inventing logical path forward based on hallucinated information. Scope Misinterpretation happens when the model misunderstands the required granularity or intent of the question, particularly for counting or classification tasks. (2023) Limitations of Open-Ended Grounding Metrics In this section, we visualize why standard open-ended evaluation metrics (Bounding Box IoU and Distance Thresholds) introduce significant noise into agentic evaluation, and how AgentVQAs MCQ format resolves this ambiguity. As illustrated in Figure 4, open-ended metrics often force trade-off: loose thresholds or large bounding boxes allow false positives on irregular shapes (like the scissors), while strict thresholds punish valid actions on large elements (like the mouse). AgentVQA circumvents this by transforming the continuous coordinate space into discrete decision problem, where distractors are programmatically ensured to be incorrect (e.g., outside the ground truth bounds) yet plausible enough to test precision. Implications and Suggestions for Practitioners AgentVQA provides unique diagnostic data unavailable in general VQA benchmarks. Based on the granular failure modes identified in our experiments, we offer the following concrete recommendations for future agentic model design and training: Accelerate Model Iteration: AgentVQA provides scalable testbed for cross-domain performance. Evaluating complex agentic questions with reasoning model judge (generating around 2,000 tokens per decision) requires millions of output tokens for single pass. AgentVQA mitigates these massive computational costs by enabling rapid, deterministic scoring for faster development cycles. Improve Visual Grounding: Among the analyzed incorrect Web Agents predictions from Gemini 3.1 Pro, 78% were classified as grounding errors: the model understood the goal but failed to locate the 19 appropriate UI element. This identifies UI localization as prominent failure mode in the analyzed sample and suggests it as target for improvement. Adopt Adaptive Inference: Since reasoning models often underperform on perception tasks, we recommend adaptive architectures that decouple fast, robust perception modules (for spatial awareness) from expensive Chain-of-Thought (for planning) to prevent Thinking Loops. Implement Domain-Specific Curricula: The lack of correlation between general VQA and agentic performance suggests generic tuning is inadequate. Our granular error profiles suggest move toward domain-specific curriculum learning, targeting 3D spatial data for Robotics versus causal reasoning for Games. Deploy Offline Safety Gates: We propose using AgentVQA as standardized diagnostic filter to detect critical reliability risks such as hallucinations and recursive loops before deploying agents into high-stakes, open-ended environments. Analysis of "Thinking Loops" as Failure Mode During our analysis of different reasoning models, we identified some models like GLM-4.1V-Thinking getting stuck in repetitive cycle of reasoning without making any forward progress. For instance, when analyzing one models reasoning process, we observed it getting stuck in the loop shown below: <think> The person in the video is seen placing small triangle on the table. The next shape that the person places is large circle. The person then places another triangle next to the circle. The person then places another triangle next to the circle and the triangle. The person then places another triangle next to the circle and the triangle. The person then places another triangle next to the circle and the triangle........ Error mode annotation. We use Gemini 3.1 Pro to categorize model failures into predefined error modes (Section G). All automated assignments were manually verified on random subset of 100 samples. Evaluation Prompt We use standard, simple prompt structure that provides the model with the question, any relevant context such as action history, and concludes by instructing it to output only the single letter corresponding to its final choice. The sample prompt structure is mentioned below (Action History would be removed in case of non-trajectory based questions). The prompt below illustrates the Web Agents version of the standard evaluation template, which is adapted slightly across domains to accommodate differences in visual inputs, task context, and question types:

sections.content: This is the standard template used for model evaluation. Placeholders like {episode_goal} are replaced with the specific data for each question. Goal: {episode_goal} Action History: {action_history if action_history.strip() else "No previous actions"} Question: {question} Options: {options_text} Based on the provided screenshot, goal, action history, and question, select the single best option from the list above. IMPORTANT: Your response must be EXACTLY one character (A, B, C, or D) with no other text, explanation, or formatting. Answer: 21 Hard Negative Generation Prompt This is the primary prompt template used to generate hard negative distractors for datasets like AITW; we use similar but tailored schema for other datasets requiring transformation. Context: The UI screenshot has dimensions {width}x{height} pixels. The image provided has green dot marking the location of the correct action if it is tap. The correct action is: {correct_action_string} Goal: {goal} Previous Actions (History): {history if history else "This is the first step."} Your Task: Generate three distinct and plausible but incorrect distractor actions. These distractors should be designed to confuse tester. Use mix of the following strategies: 1. Near-Miss: An action of the same type as the correct one but slightly off (e.g., tapping right next to the correct button). 2. Semantic-Confusion: An action on different but visually or functionally similar element (e.g., tapping blacktooth Settings when Wi-Fi Settings is correct). Supported Action Formats (Use these formats EXACTLY): Tap: [x, y] (where and are integer pixel coordinates) Swipe: DIRECTION (where DIRECTION is one of Up, Down, Left, Right) Type: text to type (where text to type is plausible but incorrect string) Button: ACTION (where ACTION is one of Press Back, Press Home, Press Enter) Important Rules: Do NOT generate the correct answer ({correct_action_string}). Ensure all tap coordinates are within the image bounds (width: {width}, height: {height}). For "Tap" distractors, analyze the image to choose locations that are genuinely incorrect but tempting. Generate diverse set of three distractors. You also need to ensure that for near miss in tap the point is actually negative. Respond ONLY with valid JSON object in the following format: {"distractors": ["ACTION_TYPE: value", "ACTION_TYPE: value", "ACTION_TYPE: value"]} 22 Error Mode Annotation Prompt The following prompt is used to have Gemini 3.1 Pro assign specific error mode to models incorrect prediction; the prompt provides full context about the question and the models failure, along with detailed taxonomy of all possible error modes and their definitions. We present the Robotics-specific prompt as an example; analogous prompts tailored to each domain and its corresponding error-mode taxonomy are used for the other four domains. You are an expert AI agent evaluator specializing in embodied robotics and robotic reasoning tasks. Your task is to analyze why vision-language model failed on specific question and categorize the failure. M.1 CONTEXT QUESTION: {question} QUESTION TYPE: {question_type} NUMBER OF IMAGES: {num_images} DATASET: {dataset_name} M.2 VISUAL ANALYSIS Some description about the expected image scene. M.3 FAILURE DETAILS MODELS PREDICTION: {model_prediction} CORRECT ANSWER: {correct_answer} MODELS REASONING: {reasoning (if available)} TASK Analyze the models failure in this embodied robotics reasoning task. Consider whether the model correctly understood the spatial relationships, identified objects and their attributes, predicted action outcomes, handled quantitative aspects, comprehended the instruction, and mapped its reasoning to the correct output. Focus on identifying the root cause using the specialized robotics error modes below. ERROR MODES {A detailed list of all error modes and their definitions is provided here.} Respond with JSON object containing the error_mode and brief justification for your choice. If you think that none of the error_modes apply then write NaN in error mode and justify in justification and also propose some new error mode in the justification and explain how this one aligns well with this sample as compared to others. It is not always necessary that an error mode applies so you can output NaN along with the justification and closest error mode from list and your idea of error mode for this.
